name: there
advice: Pick the one task that moves your main goal. Do it before email.
Before touching model code, look at 50 raw samples. Data bugs hide where you never look.
Overfit one batch first. If loss won't go to zero on 8 examples, the bug is in the pipeline.
Check the loss at init. Wrong starting loss means wrong labels, wrong logits or wrong scaling.
Fix the seed and run twice. If the numbers differ, you can't trust any comparison yet.
Don't be a hero: copy the closest working recipe before inventing a new one.
Add one change per experiment. Two changes at once teach you nothing.
A baseline you didn't run is a guess. Run the dumbest baseline before the clever model.
Plot predictions, not just metrics. One wrong-looking example beats ten decimal places.
Write the hypothesis before launching the run. Then you know what result would change your mind.
Log the exact command, git hash and config with every result. Future you will not remember.
Silent failures are the norm in deep learning. Assume the run is wrong until a check says otherwise.
Change batch size, retune the learning rate. They are not independent knobs.
Tune the learning rate first. It matters more than almost any other hyperparameter.
Visualise what goes into the model right before the forward pass, after all augmentation.
If a result seems too good, look for leakage before you celebrate.
Group your CV splits by patient or study. Leakage across splits inflates everything.
Kill the experiment that can't change the paper. Compute is cheap, your attention is not.
Keep a one-line lab notebook entry per run: what, why, result, next.
Ablations answer reviewer questions before they ask them. Plan the table first.
A negative result written down is worth more than a positive one you can't reproduce.
Write the contributions list first. If it's empty, the paper isn't ready.
Writing is research. Start the paper to find out what you actually know.
Skip the 'rest of this paper is organised as follows' paragraph. Nobody misses it.
Go straight to the idea. Readers don't need your path to it.
Put the key result in the abstract with a number, not an adjective.
Every figure caption should be readable without the main text.
One paragraph, one point. If you can't name the point, cut the paragraph.
Write the ugly first draft fast. Editing a bad page beats staring at a blank one.
Cut 'very', 'novel', 'significantly' unless a p-value backs it.
Read your abstract out loud. If you stumble, a reviewer will too.
Send a near-final draft to someone you cite. Ask if you describe their work fairly.
Show a draft to a non-expert. Where they get lost is where reviewers skim.
Giving credit to others costs you nothing and buys trust.
Write 30 minutes before checking email. The inbox will still be there.
Set a word target, not a time target: 300 words, then you're allowed to stop.
Stop mid-sentence at the end of a session. Tomorrow starts itself.
Steady daily writing beats weekend binges. Small and every day wins.
Turn each reviewer comment into a to-do, then quote and answer it point by point.
Wait a day before replying to harsh reviews. Respond to the substance, not the tone.
In a rebuttal, give line, table and figure numbers. Make the reviewer's job easy.
Assume the AC reads only the reviews and your rebuttal. Make it self-contained.
Never apologise for the old version in a rebuttal. State what you improved.
Push back on a reviewer politely and with evidence when they are wrong.
Each criticism is a pointer to something you could explain better.
Unread work earns no credit. Make the result easy to find and hard to ignore.
Work on an important problem. Ask yourself what the most important problem in your field is, and why you aren't on it.
Keep your attention on one real problem long enough for your subconscious to chew on it.
Read less, but better. One paper understood beats ten skimmed.
Open-door hours are for ideas, closed-door hours are for output. Know which one you're in.
Knowledge compounds like interest. One extra focused hour a day adds up over a PhD.
Build your own style. Copying others' taste caps you at their level.
Schedule deep work on the calendar like a meeting you can't move.
Decide where, how long, and the rules before a focus block starts.
Measure hours of deep work, not hours at the desk.
Get comfortable being bored. Reaching for the phone in every gap trains distraction.
Batch shallow work into one slot. Email, forms and Slack get the leftover energy.
Pick a fixed daily deep-work time. A rhythm beats willpower.
Shut down at a set time with a written plan for tomorrow. Then actually stop.
Close every tab not related to the current task.
Phone in another room during focus blocks. Out of reach, out of mind.
If a task takes under two minutes, do it now. Otherwise schedule it.
Eat the frog: do the hardest task first, while your brain is fresh.
Write tomorrow's top three tasks before you leave today.
If it isn't on the calendar, it isn't happening.
Say no to new commitments by default this week. Protect the paper.
A vague task never starts. Rewrite it as the first physical action.
Timebox exploration. 30 minutes on a rabbit hole, then decide in or out.
Review the week every Friday: what shipped, what slipped, what to drop.
Progress is visible or it didn't happen. Commit, push, send.
Momentum beats motivation. Do five minutes and the rest usually follows.
Reduce the cost of starting: leave the file open and the cursor where you stopped.
Context switching costs about 20 minutes each time. Finish before switching.
Notifications off. Nothing in academia needs an answer within an hour.
Ask for help at the 20-minute mark, not the 2-day mark.
When blocked, write the question as if posting to a forum. Often the answer appears.
Read the error message fully before searching for it.
Reproduce the bug before you fix it. Otherwise you can't prove you fixed it.
Delete code you don't need. The best line of code is the one never written.
Make it work, make it right, make it fast, in that order.
Commit small and often with messages that say why, not what.
Name things for what they mean, not how they're computed.
A script you'll run twice deserves a README line.
Version your data like code. Know which CSV produced which number.
Automate the thing you've done by hand three times.
Write the test that would have caught today's bug.
Prefer boring tools you know over shiny tools you're learning under deadline.
Check disk, GPU and tmux before launching. Failed launches waste hours, not minutes.
Read the diff before you commit. Every time.
Never put PHI in a commit, a log or a screenshot.
Back up the result files the moment they exist.
Document the decision, not just the code. Why beats what.
Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
Stand up and walk for a few minutes every hour. Your back and your thinking both reset.
Monitor at eye level, feet flat, forearms parallel to the floor.
Drink a glass of water now. Fatigue often starts as mild dehydration.
No coffee within about 9 hours of bedtime. Late caffeine steals sleep you won't notice losing.
Sleep is a performance tool, not a reward. Protect 7 to 8 hours.
A 10-minute walk beats another 10 minutes staring at a stuck problem.
Get daylight in the first hour after waking. It anchors your sleep tonight.
Lunch away from the screen. Eating at the desk is neither rest nor work.
Shoulders down, jaw unclenched, breathe out slowly. Then continue.
Tired brains make expensive bugs. Stop before you're running on fumes.
Move your body daily. Exercise is the cheapest cognitive enhancer you have.
Keep the evening screen dim and the last hour offline.
Burnout comes from no recovery, not from hard work. Schedule the rest too.
Send your advisor the update before they ask for it.
Bring a proposed answer, not just a problem, to every meeting.
End each meeting with who does what by when.
Write the email so the reply can be one word: yes or no.
Keep emails to five sentences or fewer.
Thank one collaborator specifically today. Specific thanks lands.
Tell people what you're working on. Opportunities find visible work.
A talk is an ad for your paper. One message, told three ways.
Give the talk out loud twice before the real one.
One idea per slide. If you need bullets, you need two slides.
Start the talk with the problem the audience already feels.
Put your best example on slide two, not slide twenty.
Finish the talk early. Nobody ever complained a talk ended on time.
Prepare three questions you dread and answer them now.
At a conference, meet three people whose papers you read. Ask about their next project.
Follow up a new contact within 48 hours or the connection fades.
Apply for the thing even if you meet 70 percent of the criteria.
Keep a brag file: every win, award and positive comment, with the date.
Update your CV the day something happens, not the week before a deadline.
Your network is the people you've helped. Help someone today.
Your thesis is the papers you've already published plus glue. Keep publishing.
Write the thesis chapter while the paper is fresh, not two years later.
Count backwards from the defense: which paper must be submitted this month?
Deadlines drive output. Pick the next venue and put the date on the wall.
Submit to a good-enough venue rather than polish forever for the perfect one.
Good research taste is knowing what not to do.
Ask 'so what?' after every result. If the answer is weak, it's not the headline.
Prefer the experiment that could falsify your claim.
Simple methods that work beat complex methods that almost work.
State limitations before reviewers do. It earns trust.
Make one figure that tells the whole story, then build the paper around it.
Every number in the paper should trace to a file you can open today.
Clinicians care about workflow and errors, not your loss curve. Frame results for them.
Report confidence intervals. A point estimate alone invites doubt.
Compare against the strongest baseline, not the easiest one to beat.
Read one paper outside your subfield this week. Ideas cross borders.
Skim the abstract, figures and conclusion first. Read the rest only if it earns it.
Keep a running list of open questions. Good projects grow from it.
Your future self is a collaborator. Leave them clean notes.
Discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want now.
You don't rise to your goals, you fall to your systems. Fix the system.
Hard work on the wrong thing is still the wrong thing. Check direction weekly.
Comparison steals focus. Measure yourself against last month's you.
Finished and submitted beats perfect and pending.
The first draft is for you. The second is for the reader.
If you're avoiding a task, make it smaller until it's not scary.
Celebrate the submit button, then start the next one tomorrow.
Inspect actual model inputs after augmentation before blaming the architecture.
Compare against a tuned simple baseline under the same compute budget.
Write the predicted outcome of an ablation before you launch it.
Fit preprocessing on training data, then apply it unchanged elsewhere.
Choose the primary metric before you inspect competing results.
Keep the test set out of prompt selection and threshold tuning.
Repeat promising runs across seeds before calling a small gain reliable.
Bootstrap patients, not correlated frames, when estimating patient-level confidence intervals.
Use a paired significance test when models are evaluated on the same patients.
Report the confidence interval for the performance difference, not just each model separately.
Check precision and recall when rare positives make ROC AUC look reassuring.
Inspect calibration before treating model scores as probabilities.
Verify that every intended trainable layer receives a finite gradient.
Match the checkpoint to its exact configuration before rerunning evaluation.
Remove one component at a time when testing which component earned its complexity.
Account for multiple comparisons before celebrating the best of many tests.
Separate uncertainty from patient sampling from variability across training seeds.
Keep every study from the same patient in a single split.
Audit report-derived labels for negation, uncertainty, and historical findings.
Ask a radiologist to adjudicate disagreements without seeing the model prediction first.
Define which clinical decision a correct prediction would change.
Test on a genuinely independent site before claiming transportability.
Check whether scanner or site markers predict the target without anatomy.
Review angiography frame order and contrast phase before sampling clips.
Verify that cropping preserves the vessel segment needed for the task.
Check whether left-right flips invalidate laterality labels or report text.
Include poor-quality studies in evaluation when deployment will encounter them.
Count eligible patients lost at each exclusion step.
State the reference standard and who established it.
Measure reader agreement before treating every label disagreement as model failure.
Ask clinicians which false negatives are most costly, then inspect those cases.
Check performance across acquisition protocols and report subgroup sample sizes.
Estimate predictive value at a prevalence relevant to the intended clinical setting.
Audit image-report pairing when one encounter contains several studies.
Write the central claim in one sentence before reorganizing the paper.
Make the abstract report a concrete result with its evaluation setting.
Give each paragraph one job and remove sentences that do another.
Order the results around research questions rather than experiment launch dates.
Make figure labels readable at the size the journal will print.
State sample size, uncertainty, and comparison details in the caption.
Replace a vague claim of improvement with the measured change and metric.
Explain why the closest prior method does not answer your specific question.
Put the evidence beside the claim it supports.
Define an acronym only if you will use it enough to justify the burden.
Use the same name for each dataset and model throughout the manuscript.
Replace a long methods sentence with the actual sequence of operations.
Keep limitations specific enough that a reader knows where the result may fail.
Read the introduction without citations to check whether its argument still connects.
Draft a small worked example when notation hides the main idea.
Check every number in the abstract against the final results table.
Ask a colleague outside your project to identify the contribution from the first page.
Turn each reviewer concern into a separate item with an owner and status.
Answer the concern in the first sentence of each rebuttal response.
Point reviewers to the exact revised section, table, or line.
Fix a misunderstanding in the manuscript as well as in the rebuttal.
Distinguish evidence you already have from experiments you are proposing.
Concede a valid criticism without burying it under a defense of unrelated work.
Explain why a requested experiment would or would not test the disputed claim.
Remove irritated language before sending a response to coauthors.
Prioritize comments that threaten validity before polishing minor wording.
Check that the revised manuscript delivers every change promised in the response.
When reviewing, summarize the actual contribution before judging it.
Separate flaws that invalidate a result from improvements that would extend it.
Tie each major criticism to a specific claim or passage.
Do not demand your preferred method unless its absence undermines the conclusion.
State where your expertise is limited so the editor can weigh your review.
Check the venue policy before placing a confidential manuscript into any AI tool.
Make your recommendation consistent with the severity of the concerns you listed.
Name the bottleneck that prevents this problem from being solved today.
Choose a project whose failure would still teach you something useful.
Test the assumption most likely to kill the project before building the full pipeline.
Write a stopping rule before the next month of experiments begins.
Ask whether the proposed novelty changes an outcome anyone cares about.
Read the figures and methods before trusting the abstract's explanation.
Record one usable idea and one unresolved weakness after reading a paper.
Trace an important claim back to the experiment that originally supported it.
Reserve time for questions your current benchmark cannot answer.
Cut a project when its remaining value no longer justifies its remaining cost.
Separate a missing engineering capability from a missing scientific insight.
Choose the smallest study that can distinguish your competing explanations.
Write down what evidence would make you abandon your favorite hypothesis.
Estimate annotation and access costs before committing to a data-hungry idea.
Revisit a neglected failure case before adding another fashionable module.
Ask whether your advantage is data access, domain insight, or a better method.
Stop reading when you can state the next experiment and its purpose.
Put the hardest reasoning task in the part of the day when you think most clearly.
Close the inbox before starting a task that needs sustained attention.
Define a visible output for this work block before opening more tabs.
Leave your phone beyond easy reach while you work.
Group short meetings so they do not fragment every open hour.
Start the avoided task with five minutes of concrete work.
Write distracting ideas on a scratch list and return to the current task.
Choose one active deliverable when three half-finished tasks are competing.
Set a time limit for troubleshooting before you seek another pair of eyes.
Use a job-completion alert instead of repeatedly refreshing the training log.
End a work session by writing the exact next action.
Move routine formatting to a period when your concentration is lower.
Turn a vague task into a verb and an object you can finish today.
Check whether reorganizing your tools is delaying the work they are meant to support.
Protect a writing appointment with the same seriousness as an external meeting.
Decide when to check messages instead of letting notifications set the schedule.
When interrupted, note your current reasoning before switching tasks.
Commit a working checkpoint before making a risky refactor.
Save the launch command, code commit, and environment with each run.
Test checkpoint recovery before trusting a multi-day training job.
Use tmux for an allowed interactive remote job, and follow cluster scheduler rules.
Confirm the host, GPU, and output directory before launching a costly run.
Make scripts fail loudly when required files or arguments are missing.
Write a regression test for a bug that changed your results.
Version dataset manifests so a filename change cannot silently redefine an experiment.
Keep raw data immutable and write derived outputs to separate locations.
Test metric code on a tiny example with an answer you can calculate by hand.
Make rerunning a pipeline safe when some outputs already exist.
Inspect a git diff for credentials and patient information before committing.
Replace a repeated manual command sequence with a documented script.
Check available disk space before a job starts producing large checkpoints.
Verify a backup by restoring a small sample from it.
Profile the slow stage before rewriting code for speed.
Archive the artifacts behind a published result before cleaning old runs.
Bring your advisor a decision, the evidence, and your recommendation.
Put the requested action and deadline near the top of an email.
Send a short agenda early enough for collaborators to prepare.
End a meeting with named owners and dates for the agreed actions.
Share a blocker while there is still time for someone to help.
Ask a clinician to explain an unfamiliar term using a real workflow example.
Separate what you observed from what you infer in a progress update.
Rehearse a talk aloud with a timer rather than silently reading slides.
Make each slide title state the point the audience should remember.
Explain a graph's axes before discussing the pattern in it.
Prepare a short answer about the strongest limitation of your study.
Cut poster text until someone can find the main result while standing back.
Agree on authorship roles before collaboration creates conflicting expectations.
Confirm ambiguous feedback in your own words before implementing it.
Send collaborators a specific question instead of asking for general thoughts.
Tell a collaborator early when a deadline is slipping and propose a revised plan.
Pause after a question so you answer what was asked rather than your rehearsed version.
Ask a conference speaker one question grounded in their actual results.
Follow up with a new contact using the specific idea you discussed.
Keep a record of contributions while the details are still fresh.
Tailor an application around the problems the group actually works on.
Ask a potential mentor how they give feedback and resolve stalled projects.
Request recommendation letters early and provide evidence the writer can use.
Update your CV when work changes status, not only when an application is due.
Explain your own contribution clearly in every project description.
Prepare an interview example of a technical mistake and how you corrected it.
Ask former lab members about mentorship before accepting a position.
Choose service work that fits a stated priority and a realistic time budget.
Decline a request clearly when accepting it would break an existing commitment.
Keep a public project summary that an interested researcher can understand quickly.
Discuss career options before the final months of funding force the decision.
Offer a useful paper, introduction, or technical answer when building a professional connection.
Compare roles on daily work and mentorship as well as title and institution.
Look away from the screen periodically and let your eyes focus farther away.
Adjust screen glare and text size when reading requires squinting or leaning forward.
Bring the keyboard close enough that your shoulders can relax.
Support your feet and lower back while seated.
Change position regularly instead of searching for one posture to hold all day.
Get up for a brief walk after a long stretch of sitting.
Put activity on your calendar toward 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week.
Schedule muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days each week.
Protect enough time for at least seven hours of sleep on a regular basis.
Keep your sleep and wake times reasonably consistent across the week.
Move caffeine earlier if it is delaying or disrupting your sleep.
Keep drinking water accessible and respond to thirst during long work sessions.
Seek help for persistent pain instead of repeatedly working through it.
Take a brief pause and slow your breathing when tension starts driving your decisions.
Discuss sustained exhaustion with your advisor and a health professional before it becomes your normal routine.
If sleep problems persist, seek care rather than relying on another productivity workaround.
List the remaining graduation requirements using the university's current checklist.
Agree with your committee on what constitutes a complete thesis.
Map each thesis chapter to its claim, evidence, and unfinished work.
Draft the connecting argument between papers before assembling the dissertation.
Work backward from the filing deadline to committee review and revision dates.
Ask committee members about availability before choosing a defense date.
Finish a rough chapter before polishing its opening page.
Mark missing thesis details explicitly so they do not halt the whole draft.
Separate required graduation work from optional extensions of the research.
Track chapter readiness using concrete criteria rather than a percentage guess.
Check dissertation formatting while revisions are still cheap.
Prepare a defense answer for why each major methodological choice was reasonable.
Arrange a mock defense with someone willing to challenge your assumptions.
Leave time after the defense for corrections and administrative signatures.
Document datasets, code, and unfinished work for the person who inherits the project.
Choose one finishable thesis task before taking on another new idea.
Treat a failed run as evidence only after ruling out an implementation error.
Compare your current work with your earlier work before comparing it with someone else's highlight.
Separate a rejected paper from a judgment about your ability to do research.
Keep a record of corrected mistakes so the same lesson does not cost you twice.
Replace self-criticism with a description of the behavior you will change next.
When progress feels invisible, inspect the artifacts you completed this week.
Do the planned task before renegotiating it because your mood changed.
Accept a smaller honest claim when the evidence does not support the larger one.
Ask for help when pride is costing more time than the problem itself.
Do not let money already spent decide whether another experiment is worthwhile.
Choose a sustainable weekly pace over a burst that makes the next week unusable.
Notice when defending your idea has replaced testing it.
Keep commitments small enough that you can reliably honor them.
Write down a setback's practical consequences before assuming the worst.
Credit collaborators explicitly when their work made your result possible.
Spend effort on the next controllable decision when the outcome is already out of your hands.

default: Pick one task, set a 50-minute block, do the smallest first step.
